passage:
In the hostel sick room, Urmila lay under a thin blanket with a fever while her phone kept buzzing. Darshan, a senior from her department, had forwarded the same message four times: "Herbal kadha CURED my cousin's fever the very next morning. Doctors won't tell you this." Then a photo of a steaming cup. Then: "Have you tried it yet??"
Urmila felt pressured and a bit guilty, as if not trying it meant she didn't want to get better. Her roommate brought a cup from the mess anyway, and she sipped it because it was warm.
The campus doctor, checking on her that evening, glanced at the screen. "Fevers like this usually settle with rest, whatever people drink," she said. "Tell me if it keeps going or you feel worse."
Two days later, fever gone, Darshan wrote: "See? The kadha worked!" Urmila typed a reply, deleted it, and sent a thumbs-up.

qa.q: What did Darshan's forwarded message claim?
qa.a: That herbal kadha cured a cousin's fever the very next morning.

qa.q: How did the repeated messages make Urmila feel?
qa.a: Pressured and a bit guilty, as if not trying the kadha meant she didn't want to get better.

qa.q: What could Urmila say back to Darshan without starting a fight?
qa.a: She could thank Darshan for caring and say the doctor told her fevers like hers usually settle with rest, so nobody can tell what the kadha did.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Urmila's recovery?
qa.a: As proof the kadha worked, because she got better after drinking it, without considering that the fever would likely have gone anyway.

grounding: It shows a student on the receiving end of forwarded cure claims whose timing sounds convincing but ignores natural recovery.

passage:
Dear Vijay Mama,
Thank you for all the messages this week. I know you send them because you worry about Mummy's back. The one about the leaf paste says a man in Salem was walking normally two days after using it, and the video looks so real.
But I've been thinking. Mummy's back pain also eases by itself sometimes, after rest, and then comes back. If she had tried the paste in a good week, we'd have thanked the paste. And the man in Salem, we don't know what else he did, or whether he saw a doctor too.
This is hard for me, because I don't want to sound rude to you, and part of me wants the paste to work. Mummy is seeing her doctor on Friday, and I'll ask about it there.
With love,
Preeti

qa.q: What does the message about the leaf paste claim?
qa.a: That a man in Salem was walking normally two days after using it.

qa.q: Why does Preeti feel this letter is hard to write?
qa.a: Preeti doesn't want to sound rude to Mama, and part of Preeti wants the paste to work, so doubting it feels uncomfortable.

qa.q: What is sensible about Preeti's plan?
qa.a: Taking the question to Mummy's doctor on Friday puts the decision with someone who knows her back, instead of trusting a video.

qa.q: How might Vijay Mama feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He might feel a little corrected but also loved, since Preeti starts by thanking him and says the messages come from worry. 🤍

grounding: It shows a student receiving forwarded cure stories whose timing sounds convincing while ignoring natural ups and downs and other causes.

passage: Santosh, remember that rash on my arms in first year? Here's Lalit's official confession about it. Within a day, the family group was full of forwards. Chitti sent one about a neem and turmeric paste: "Boy in Madurai, skin clear in one week!" Then Periappa sent the same thing with a before-and-after photo. Then three more relatives. Every morning I woke up to "Did you try it?" I felt like if I didn't, I was insulting everyone who cared. So I tried it, and I also went to the college clinic because it itched like crazy. The doctor said it was probably a reaction to the new detergent. I switched soap, kept using the paste, and it cleared. Chitti still says it was the paste. Honestly? I can't tell. Nobody can, from that.

qa.q: What did the college clinic doctor say caused the rash?
qa.a: Probably a reaction to the new detergent.

qa.q: How did the flood of forwards make Lalit feel?
qa.a: Lalit felt that not trying the paste would insult everyone who cared, so the messages felt more like pressure than help.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that was wise, and what made the result unclear?
qa.a: Going to the clinic and switching soap was sensible, but using the paste at the same time means nobody can tell what cleared the rash.

qa.q: Why does Chitti keep believing it was the paste?
qa.a: The rash cleared after the paste was used, and Chitti had sent the tip out of care, so seeing it 'work' feels like proof.

grounding: It shows a student receiving viral cure forwards whose before-and-after timing ignores other causes like the change of soap.

passage:
I'm Vishal, and I share a desk with Usha in our second-year chemistry lab. Last week she came in with her voice almost gone and a scarf round her neck.
By the first break her phone had buzzed maybe fifteen times. She showed me one message from her aunt: "Tulsi-ginger leaf water CURED a boy in two days! Doctors don't want you to know." Another from a family group had a photo of a smiling man and "Took it at night, fine by morning."
Usha kept reading them and then putting the phone face down. She said, "Everyone's so sure. What if I don't try it and it gets worse?" She looked tired and a bit cornered.
On Thursday she went to the campus clinic anyway. By Monday her voice was back. The aunt sent another message: "See? The leaf water!" Usha hadn't drunk it.

qa.q: What did the aunt's message say the leaf water did?
qa.a: It said tulsi-ginger leaf water "CURED a boy in two days".

qa.q: What was Usha worried about as the messages kept coming?
qa.a: She was worried that ignoring such confident messages might make her throat worse, and she seemed tired and a bit cornered by all the pressure.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Usha, and what does the ending show about the forwards?
qa.a: Going to the campus clinic worked; the aunt crediting leaf water Usha never drank shows how timing alone can make a cure story sound true.

qa.q: What is it like for Usha to receive so many forwards while she is unwell?
qa.a: It adds pressure and guilt when Usha just wants to rest, because each confident message makes her feel she is doing something wrong by not trying it.

grounding: It shows a student receiving forwards claiming a herb cured someone right after taking it, while timing ignores natural recovery and other causes.

passage:
Monday: Kamal, twenty, limped home from football with a sore knee. By night his Rukmini Chachi had sent three voice notes and a forward: "Warm herbal oil, one night, boy in Madurai walked perfectly next day!"
Wednesday: The knee felt better. Kamal had rested, skipped practice and kept it up on a pillow. He'd also rubbed on the oil once, to keep Chachi happy. Chachi sent a thumbs-up and "Told you, the oil!" Kamal almost believed it. Then he thought: which part had worked, the rest or the oil? The Madurai boy's story said nothing about rest.
Saturday: A physiotherapist at the sports centre checked the knee, said it was a mild strain healing on its own, and gave him exercises. Kamal texted Chachi: "Thank you for caring. The physio says rest did most of it." Chachi replied with a single flower.

qa.q: What did the forward say about the boy in Madurai?
qa.a: It said the boy "walked perfectly next day" after one night of warm herbal oil.

qa.q: What made Kamal almost believe the oil had worked, and what made him doubt it?
qa.a: The knee felt better soon after the oil, so the timing was convincing; then he remembered he had also rested, skipped practice and kept it up, and wondered which one had helped.

qa.q: Which choice was the turning point for Kamal?
qa.a: Seeing the physiotherapist, who explained the strain was healing on its own and gave him exercises, instead of crediting the oil because of timing.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Chachi feel when she reads Kamal's reply?
qa.a: Chachi may feel a little deflated that the oil wasn't the answer, but also touched that Kamal thanked her for caring, as her flower suggests.

grounding: It shows a student receiving a forward that claims an oil cured someone right after use, while the timing hides natural recovery and rest.
